forces: Two violins, two violas and two cellos
performers: Hollywood String Quartet (Felix Slatkin and Paul Shure, violins; Paul Robyn, viola; Eleanor Aller, cello); Alvin Dinkin, viola; Kurt Reher, cello
intro: D major is the man’s answer: he accepts the woman and her child. The second side of the Hollywood String Quartet’s Verklärte Nacht carries the six players from that broad declaration into muted moonlight and a quiet close.

sections.label: A · The cellos answer in D major
sections.mNote: Violas and cellos begin the man’s reply

sections.label: B · Muted strings and harmonics
sections.mNote: F♯ major, muted runs and lightly touched strings

sections.label: C · Violin and cello in dialogue
sections.mNote: Earlier themes return among the six players

sections.label: Coda · The walking theme in major
sections.mNote: The opening walk meets the man’s answering theme

sections.label: Coda · High violin, flowing inner strings
sections.mNote: The second violin keeps moving beneath long upper notes

cues.title: An answer in D major
cues.text: Violas and cellos open a broad D-major chord, marked Sehr breit und langsam — very broadly and slowly. The first cello begins an expressive line. In Dehmel’s poem, the man accepts the child his companion is carrying.
cues.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), p. 26, bars 229–240; Schoenberg’s programme notes (1950), example 10. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Moonlight under the mutes
cues.text: The strings put on mutes. Quick violin runs cross the still, pale notes of harmonics, made by touching the strings lightly. The key is F♯ major; Schoenberg identifies this passage with the beauty of the moonlight.
cues.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), p. 27, bars 249–250: six-sharp signature, mutes and harmonics. Schoenberg’s 1950 programme notes, example 11. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Violin and cello together
cues.text: A violin and cello duet grows out of the muted passage. Earlier phrases reappear around it, with new accompaniments. The six players have room both for the man’s broad reply and for the woman’s remembered distress.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s programme notes (1950), examples 12–16, describe the violin–cello duet and the return and development of earlier themes. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The poet forgets his poem
cues.text: After hearing the sextet, Dehmel writes to Schoenberg on 12 December 1912. He has meant to trace his poem through the music, but soon forgets the task: the six strings hold his attention on their own.
cues.evidence: Richard Dehmel to Schoenberg, 12 December 1912, quoted in Therese Muxeneder’s work essay. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: Six players before the orchestra
cues.text: Schoenberg later makes Verklärte Nacht into a work for string orchestra, adding double basses in 1917 and revising the arrangement in 1943. Here the original six players remain: every violin, viola and cello part belongs to one person.
cues.evidence: Arnold Schönberg Center work essay distinguishes the original sextet from the 1917 and 1943 string-orchestra versions and identifies the added double-bass part. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: The walk in major
cues.text: The coda brings back the opening walking theme in the major, with the man’s answering theme set against it. The two people in Dehmel’s poem are still walking beneath the same moon.
cues.evidence: Therese Muxeneder’s work essay identifies the opening motif in major and the fourth section’s principal theme as its counterpoint in the coda; Dehmel’s final stanza returns to the night walk. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A high violin, still moving
cues.text: The first violin holds long notes above the second violin’s running figures. Violas and cellos fill the space between them. Even at the softest end of the piece, the inner parts keep flowing until all six instruments settle into D major.
cues.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), pp. 50–51, bars 409–418: sustained first violin, running second violin and final D-major chord. https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/manuskripte.php?werke_id=420&id_quelle=1213&herkunft=allewerke
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Mutes after the pause
transitions.from: A · The cellos answer in D major
transitions.how: A ritardando and fermata hold back the sextet before F♯ major. The violins begin muted runs; violas and cellos answer with harmonics. The broad, bowed D-major declaration has become a passage of lightly touched strings.

transitions.title: Violin and cello find a duet
transitions.to: C · Violin and cello in dialogue
transitions.how: Above the shimmering accompaniment, a new melody develops into a duet for violin and cello. Schoenberg lets the two instruments carry the longer phrases while the remaining strings keep the accompaniment moving.
transitions.evidence: Schoenberg’s programme notes (1950), examples 12–14, describe the accompaniment and violin–cello duet. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

transitions.title: The opening walk comes back
transitions.from: C · Violin and cello in dialogue
transitions.to: Coda · The walking theme in major
transitions.how: The coda recalls the opening walking motif in the major and combines it with the man’s answering melody. The six strings bring phrases from both halves of the piece into the closing pages.
transitions.evidence: Therese Muxeneder’s account of the fifth section and Schoenberg’s programme notes (1950), final paragraph. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

transitions.title: The second violin keeps flowing
transitions.from: Coda · The walking theme in major
transitions.to: Coda · High violin, flowing inner strings
transitions.how: The first violin stretches its notes above the second violin’s rapid figures. Quiet viola and cello parts fill out the harmony; the last page briefly brings back harmonics before the running figures stop on the held D-major chord.

timeline.note: Violas and cellos open the D-major answer; the first cello carries the broad melody.
The violins join the lower strings, extending the man’s D-major answer.
Muted violin runs cross the lightly touched harmonics of violas and cellos.
A violin–cello duet grows out of the moving accompaniment; earlier phrases pass among the six players.
The closing pages combine the walking theme in major with the man’s answering melody.
The first violin holds long notes above the second violin’s rapid figures, towards the final D-major chord.

composer.epithet: He removed the home key from music, kept learning from Bach and Brahms, and found room for a minuet among all twelve notes.
facts: Largely self-taught; lessons with Alexander Zemlinsky
Alban Berg and Anton Webern from 1904; later Hanns Eisler and John Cage
Prussian Academy of Arts, Berlin, 1926–33; UCLA, 1936–44
Painter; author of Harmonielehre (1911); founder of the Society for Private Musical Performances
composer.background:
At the première of Pierrot lunaire in Berlin on 16 October 1912, Albertine Zehme stood onstage in a Pierrot costume. Behind a screen, five instrumentalists watched Arnold Schoenberg conduct. They had held twenty-five ensemble rehearsals to prepare thirty-odd minutes of music in which the voice slid away from its written notes, a flute could turn into a piccolo, and a violinist had to pick up a viola. The screen concealed one of the busiest small orchestras ever assembled.

Schoenberg was born in Vienna’s Leopoldstadt in 1874 and began learning the violin as a child. His father died when he was fifteen. From 1891 to 1895 he worked in a bank, making music with friends and teaching himself from scores. Alexander Zemlinsky, whom he met through the amateur orchestra Polyhymnia, gave him lessons. Brahms showed him how a small phrase could grow by changing; Wagner showed him how long a chord could keep us waiting.
